items.title: FCM Award – The Ann MacLean Award for Outstanding Service by a
notes: Woman in Municipal Politics
Councillor Vasic opened with some remarks:

Over the past decade, I’ve popped in and out of Seven Shores, to Peter’s “office”, and I’ve come to know Lynne through Peter. Lynne, for those of you who don’t know, is a former mayor of Waterloo. For me, Lynne has come to join my other role models, like my great-grandmother through to my mom who integrated both a deep love for her family and a commitment to her family, while also working and contributing to her community. While I’ve never had the fortune of meeting her myself, I and many of us have benefitted from her staunch advocacy. My kids’ daycare remembers her and has invited Peter on her behalf to their anniversary celebration in September, because she was instrumental in getting them their space. She advanced environmental work at the City, which we continue to build on today, and she was a champion for affordable housing, before the time the situation reached its crisis today. I hope I will have a legacy that will live on in those who never meet me as well, just as she has had on me, many of you, and the community. It’s because of this legacy and the impact that I nominated her for the Federation of Canadian Municipalities Ann MacLean Award for Outstanding Service by a Woman or Non-binary Person in Municipalities, and that’s what we’re here to celebrate today.

The award recognizes retired women and non-binary municipal politicians who have shown exemplary service to their community and constituents and to mentoring women and non-binary folks who want to run for elected office. It is named in honour of FCM Past President, Ann MacLean, who led FCM’s campaign to increase the number of women in municipal politics across Canada.
The recipient is chosen by the FCM Board of Directors and is presented with the award at their Annual Conference.
Our former Mayor Lynne Woolstencroft was given this honour in 2021 posthumously; however, due to the pandemic the conference and award presentation was not held.
I wanted to thank City staff who helped organize this event, and thank you to those who wrote letters of support for the nomination.
Councillor Freeman offered further remarks on Lynne Woolstencroft’s legacy:
Lynne dedicated her life to public service, helping others and championing the environment.

She served as a school board trustee from 1970-1972, 1974-1985 and was elected chair from 1979-1982. She was elected councillor for the City of Waterloo for three terms, from 1985–1988, 1988–1991, and 1997–2000 and in 2000 she was elected as Mayor of the City of Waterloo.

During her time on Council, she was a champion of the Environment First Policy at the City which meant that environmental impacts would be thought of at the beginning of projects and initiatives. She was always interested in learning more about how to use our precious land resources more efficiently whether that was by promoting methane gas reclamation at the Region of Waterloo landfill sites or through infill housing development.

On a personal note, Lynne is the reason I chose to run as a City of Waterloo councillor in 2006. I first met Lynne when she was serving as Mayor of the City of Waterloo in 2001. I delegated to the City Council in support of a staff recommendation to allow a site-specific Official Plan Amendment to permit a childcare centre to be constructed and operated on land designated for employment use. At the time, a childcare centre was deemed a commercial use in the City zoning by-law. I explained to Council how a childcare centre was a compatible land use, because it’s important for children to be cared for close to where parents work. It would reduce travel times between work and home, it would encourage families to spend more time together during the day, it would facilitate mothers continuing to nurse their children during working hours, and it would allow for sick children to be picked up and cared for quickly.

What I faced during this delegation was an all-male Council, except for Lynne. It was clear to me that my concerns as a professional working engineer and a mother were not represented nor understood by the individuals tasked to make the decision, except for Lynne. There was talk of a deferral, requesting more information, it was a summer session of Council and they would not be meeting for at least another month. Lynne did not let this childcare centre fall through the cracks. She demanded an agreement from the members of Council to sit in an emergency meeting to receive the additional information, at which time the staff recommendation was approved.

It was during this delegation to Council that I realized that if I wanted different voices to be heard, more women, more engineers, more non-binary people, more parents, more individuals need to be decision-makers. And that if I thought I had something to offer, I should step up and put these skills on the municipal ballot through running. Lynne encouraged me, and so did Peter. You all supported me from the start to the finish, and I am so thankful for all that you shared with me and taught me.

Even though she passed away, Lynne’s legacy and work ethic continues to inspire my work as an elected official. It is for this reason, and many more, that I am thankful that Lynne Woolstencroft was the recipient of the Ann MacLean award for outstanding service by a woman in municipal politics. She was most deserving.
It is our honour to present this award to Lynne’s family this evening on behalf of the FCM Board.
Peter Woolstencroft spoke about Lynne’s legacy and her passion for education.

items.title: New Business
notes: Councillor Wright wanted to comment on the KW Chamber of Commerce awards ceremony on March 21, 2024, celebrating local volunteers, local businesses and local initiatives, like Lumen festival. One of the BIA board members, Conrad Lovell, received the Volunteer of the Year Award. It’s a great opportunity to see all the great things happening across the Region, but especially originating in the City of Waterloo.

Mayor McCabe added that for 12 of the awards, there are nearly 150 companies or organizations nominated, which really shows the breadth and strength of the business, not-for-profit, and cultural communities across Waterloo Region. She also mentioned that Waterloo resident, Tony Giovinazzo, was honoured with the Michael Follett award.

Mayor McCabe attended the Royal Canadian Legion Waterloo Branch 530 Youth Education Awards Night on Friday, March 22, 2024, where they presented approximately 75 certificates to students of all ages involved in the Royal Canadian Legion Remembrance Day Literary & Poster Contest. There is a student from Laurel Heights Secondary School whose work is in the National Competition.
Councillor Roach mentioned that today, March 25, the Hindu community recognizes the Festival of Colour, Holi. It’s important to recognize the countless contributions of Hindu Canadians to Canada.
Councillor Freeman wanted to offer her thanks for all of the hard work everyone put into the budget at the beginning of the year.

Councillor Freeman also mentioned the honorary Colonel of the Combat Engineering Regiment, the Earl of Elgin and Kincardine, celebrated his 100th birthday. The Mayor sent greetings from the City, and the Earl has handwritten his thanks. Councillor Freeman spoke about the significance of reserve regiments for Canada’s international commitments.
